paper_title: T-DIG: Text-Conditioned Diversity for Image Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Text-to-image (T2I) platforms typically return several images per prompt so users can explore different visual interpretations and choose one that matches their intent. However, T2I models are usually optimized for single-image quality which comes at a cost of multi-image diversity, limiting this exploration. Diversity is also contextual: one user wants variations in background, while another wants them in artistic style, and the same user may later want variations in clothing. The generated images should differ along whatever axis the user cares about. In this paper, we introduce T-DIG, a text-conditioned diversity framework for image generation and editing. T-DIG is an iterative framework comprising multiple modules that lets users type prompts, inspect default generations, request variations using natural language, and continue refining outputs until they're satisfied. At its core, T-DIG uses an LLM policy that produces K axis-conditioned prompts or edit instructions for a frozen generator or editor. We train this policy with GRPO using a text-conditioned diversity reward and alignment penalties. Because the image generator remains frozen, T-DIG applies to open-weight, distilled, and proprietary models. We also release the first dataset for text-conditioned prompt diversity in image generation, with the training and validation splits built from human-written axes and a test set drawn from real user interactions with T-DIG. T-DIG far exceeds baselines in improving text-conditioned diversity, while preserving base-prompt alignment across a variety of metrics and human judgements. We show that user-directed diversity exploration can be added to a wide range of image generation models, open and closed, without the need to access their weights. sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Text-to-image platforms (Midjourney, Inc., 2024; Adobe Inc., 2025) typically show four to eight images per prompt, so that the user has multiple options to choose from. However, different users may often want to see different kinds of variation, which T2I models dont typically support. We conducted human study where users were shown images for people sitting at table with laptops and books; one user asked for variation in laptops and camera angle, another wanted to see people doing different things, and third wanted to vary peoples ethnicity. Requests also ranged from being highly specific, to fairly abstract and open-ended. For dog playing in park, user asked for different dog breeds, whereas for comic-book panel..., they wanted crazy endings that would surprise them. Prior works have proposed many methods to increase diversity of image generation models, but none can accommodate for these varying scenarios. One category of diversity methods (Parmar et al., 2026; Corso et al., 2024) maximizes pairwise distance in latent embedding spaces (Fu et al., 2023; Oquab et al., 2023). These approaches make the images generically diverse but do not take the users request into consideration. Some methods do target specific proxy of diversity, for example, varying modes of an underspecified prompt (Morshed & Boddeti, 2025), the identities of people in scene (Borse et al., 2026), or demographic and geographic coverage (Askari Hemmat et al., 2024; 1Website: https://image-study.org/t-dig/

Miao et al., 2024); but they do not generalize beyond that pre-specified target. All prior methods return one output set per prompt with predetermined type of variation, as shown in Figure 1. In this paper, we treat diversity as conditional generation problem: given prompt and an axis of variation written in free-form text, produce images that differ along that axis while following the prompt. We build T-DIG, an interactive framework around this idea (Section 2). At its core, an LLM policy expands the base prompt into axis-conditioned prompts or edit instructions for frozen T2I model. We train the policy with GRPO, rewarding text-conditioned diversity measured with TPIPS (Wang et al., 2026) and penalizing loss of alignment with the base prompt. TPIPS is VLM fine-tuned on human perceptual judgments to score image similarity along free-form textspecified aspect, so it lets us measure diversity along user-specified axes. Because the T2I model stays frozen and need not be differentiable, T-DIG applies to open-weight, distilled, and API-only generators and editors. To the best of our knowledge, no existing dataset pairs prompts with user-written axes of variation. We therefore build training and validation data from HPDv2 prompts (Wu et al., 2023) with axes elicited from VLM using human-written examples in context, and test set of 405 (prompt, axis) pairs written by participants using T-DIG. Across four open-weight T2I models, T-DIG more than doubles diversity along the requested axis over i.i.d. sampling on average (2.3, and up to 3.1), while lowering alignment with the base prompt by less than 2%. Existing diversity methods (that do not condition on any axis), fall short on one side or the other: the most diverse baseline, CADS (Sadat et al., 2024), reaches 1.8 at 6% alignment drop, while Scaling Group Inference (Parmar et al., 2026) preserves alignment best (under 1% drop) but gains only 1.3, at up to 22 the sampling cost. Policies trained with open-weight models also transfer to proprietary ones on GPT Image 2, our Qwen-Image policy raises diversity about 40% more than asking GPT-5.5 to produce varied prompts along the given axis. In pairwise human evaluation, raters find T-DIGs sets more varied along the requested axis than every baselines on 6496% of instances across all T2I models in our study. Our overall contributions are: 1. Task formulation: We formulate T2I diversity as conditional generation, where users state in free-form text what should vary, from broad axes like style to prompt-specific requests no fixed taxonomy covers. 2. Interactive framework: T-DIG lets users request, control, and iteratively refine variations in natural language, by generating new sets or editing existing ones.

sections.title: 3 TRAINING
sections.content: In this section, we describe how we train the two LLM policies of the Diversity Module with GRPO, for generation and editing.

sections.title: 3.1 TRAINING DATA
sections.content: Base prompts: We start from the HPDv2 training split (Wu et al., 2023), which contains userwritten T2I prompts. After removing empty entries and exact duplicates, 103,672 unique prompts remain. We filter this pool with GPT-5.6 Luna (OpenAI, 2026a) using medium reasoning effort. The filter removes prompts that depict named real individuals, contain unsafe content, lack depictable subject, or are dominated by style and quality descriptors. prompt is retained only if the model can identify at least three meaningful axes of variation. This step retains 79.9% of the unique pool. Even after exact-duplicate removal and filtering, we find that many retained prompts are semantically similar. To reduce redundancy in training, we cluster the remaining prompts and choose sample from each, leaving roughly 20,000 prompts (filtering and clustering details in Appendix A.1). Axes: In pilot study, participants saw i.i.d. outputs for 20 prompts and wrote what they would like to vary. This is used as seed data to elicit axes of variation from VLM at scale. For each base prompt we collect above, we render i.i.d. samples with the T2I model and ask Gemini 3.8 Flash (Google, 2026) for up to four free-form axes, using the pilot instruction and responses as in-context examples. For random 10% of prompts we also add the axis overall, which supports axis-free requests in case people would like to see overall diversity. After removing malformed outputs and holding out 200 prompts for validation, the training set contains 19,765 prompts and 76,089 (prompt, axis) pairs.

sections.title: 4.1 SETUP
sections.content: T2I Models: We evaluate across open-weight, distilled, and proprietary models: Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium and Large (Stability AI, 2024), Qwen-Image-2512 (Qwen Team, 2025), and FLUX.2 [klein] 9B (distilled) (Black Forest Labs, 2026); and API models GPT Image 2, and Gemini 3.1 Flash Image (OpenAI, 2026b; Google DeepMind, 2026). For editing we use the corresponding editor of each family. We train at 512px with reduced step counts, similar to FlowGRPO (Liu et al., 2026) and evaluate at 1024px with each models recommended sampler. Prompt-set policies: We use models from the Qwen3.5 family (Team, 2026) since they have variety of model sizes available. For each T2I model we train 4B, 9B, and 35B-A3B generation policies; the base prompt and axis are fed in-context, with instructions to generate diverse prompts along the axis. Each policy is LoRA adapter (Hu et al., 2022) of rank 32 on all attention, linearattention, and MLP projections; the T2I model is never updated. Training: We use set size = 4, reward weights λ = 2, µ = 0.1 and η = 0.05, and length allowance = 20. We train LoRA adapters (rank 32) with GRPO at learning rate 2 105 without KL term, and train for 800 steps. Each update draws 8 (prompt, axis) pairs and = 8 completions per pair, so 8 = 256 images are rendered and scored in each step.

sections.content: Evaluation data: We validate on the 200 held-out prompts of Section 3.1. We also build test set from real use (Section 4.4), yielding 405 interactions, roughly 100 from each open-weight model above. For comparison with axis-agnostic methods, we evaluate T-DIG conditioned on overall on the COCO val2017 split (Lin et al., 2014) (COCO-250), where no axis is specified.

sections.title: 4.2 BASELINES
sections.content: We compare T-DIG, untrained (α = 0) and trained (α = 1), against four baselines. Untrained TDIG runs the same Qwen3.5 backbone and instruction without the adapter, which isolates the effect of GRPO. None of the baselines accepts an axis, so each returns the same set whatever the user asks to vary. Baselines draw independent initial latents, whereas T-DIG renders all prompts from one shared latent, so that differences within set come from the prompts alone. I.I.D. sampling renders the base prompt times with independent initial noise. PAG (Yun et al., 2025) fine-tunes GPT-2 with GFlowNets to sample diverse rewrites of prompt; it was trained against Stable Diffusion v1.4 and receives no axis. We decode prompts from the authors checkpoint with diverse beam search and use them to generate images from the T2I model, instead of the base prompt. PAG tests whether generic prompt diversity suffices without axis conditioning. CADS (Sadat et al., 2024) adds annealed noise to the conditioning embedding at inference time. We use it on open-weight T2I models where those embeddings are available, with the official textto-image settings τ1 = 0.6, τ2 = 0.9, = 0.25, ψ = 1. sections.title: 4.3 METRICS
sections.content: Alignment: We report VQAScore with CLIP-FlanT5-XXL (Lin et al., 2024), the probability that VQA model answers Yes to Does this figure show {prompt}?, and CLIPScore (Hessel et al., 2021) the cosine similarity between the CLIP embeddings of the image and the prompt; both are computed against the base prompt. Diversity: Our primary metric is normalized TPIPS-Vendi, TPIPSv (Wang et al., 2026; Friedman & Dieng, 2022), conditioned on the requested axis; it is the only metric here that measures variation along text-condition. TPIPS (Wang et al., 2026) is perceptual similarity metric conditioned on text prompt naming visual aspect (eg. lighting, pose), trained on human similarity judgments. Vendi score is computed from the pairwise similarities between images and gives the effective number of distinct images in set. DINOv (Oquab et al., 2023) and DreamSimv (Fu et al., 2023) measure axis-agnostic spread using self-supervised DINOv2 features and DreamSim (perceptual similarity metric trained on human judgments), respectively. Preference and aesthetics: We additionally report ImageReward (Xu et al., 2023), HPSv3 (Ma et al., 2025), and LAION-Aesthetics V2 (Schuhmann, 2022). ImageReward, and HPSv3 mix alignment with preference and are not pure aesthetic scores; the LAION score is prompt-independent.

sections.title: 4.4 HUMAN EVALUATION
sections.content: Stage 1, test-set collection: We hire participants on Prolific2 to interact with the framework we build (Section 2), where each participant makes five sets of images using one T2I model, iterating until satisfied. Each prompt and the first axis requested for it form one test pair, labeled as generate or edit request; we release later requests and refinements with each pair as additional metadata. After excluding participants who fail quality checks (eg. empty or copied comments), the test set contains 405 (prompt, axis) pairs from 58 participants across the four open-weight T2I models. 2https://www.prolific.com/

sections.content: Stage 2, ratings: For each test pair, we render sets of = 4 images with T-DIG, both trained (α = 0.5, default diversity slider position on interface) and untrained (α = 0), and with i.i.d. sampling, CADS (s = 0.25), and Scaling Group Inference (λ = 1, = 128) (we remove underperforming baselines like PAG). We collect ratings pairwise: each screen shows T-DIG next to one baseline, in random order, with the baseline rotating across pairs. separate pool of Prolific raters sees the base prompt and the requested axis, and scores each image set from 1 to 10 on how much it varies along the axis and how well it matches the prompt. Raters can mark an axis not applicable if it is not request for variation (eg. complaint about the images). Pairs with majority N/A vote are dropped, so this also validates the test set. Each pair gets three ratings (about 2,400 in total). We report two win rates by majority vote: how often T-DIG is rated more varied (diversity win rate), and how often it is rated more varied and at least as well aligned (diversity + alignment win rate).

sections.title: 5 RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
sections.content: We evaluate T-DIG on a) the interactive test set and report automatic metrics and human preference ratings  (Table 1)  ; b) COCO-250 to compare with methods designed for axis-free diversity (Figure 5), and ablate the reward  (Table 2)  . We analyze results through the research questions below. RQ1: How does T-DIG compare with baselines on text-conditioned diversity? We describe each method by its change from i.i.d. sampling on the same T2I model, and report averages/ranges across models  (Table 1)  . None of the baselines takes an axis as input, so they can only make the set vary more in general: Scaling Group Inference raises TPIPSv by +0.03 to +0.05 at 3.321.9 the denoiser cost, PAG by +0.03 to +0.09, and CADS by +0.08 to +0.17. Training-free T-DIG (α=0), which prompts the untrained policy with the axis, already matches CADS (+0.08 to +0.14), and training (α=1) roughly doubles that gain (+0.14 to +0.26). When comparing with axis-agnostic diversity metrics, we get sense of how much variation there is on-axis versus off-axis. CADS comes within 0.05 of T-DIG on DINOv and exceeds it on DreamSimv for some models, so its sets vary about as much overall, but very less of that variation lies along the requested axis, as measured by TPIPSv. An increase in diversity often comes at the cost of alignment with the base prompt. T-DIG changes VQAScore by 0.05 to +0.01, against 0.03 to 0.08 for CADS and 0.08 to 0.16 for PAG. Per +0.1 TPIPSv gained (slope in Table 1), T-DIG loses at most 0.02 VQAScore, while CADS loses up to 0.08 and PAG up to 0.41; Scaling Group Inference loses up to 0.03, but for much smaller diversity gain at much higher inference cost. With respect to preference and aesthetics, T-DIG keeps ImageReward and HPSv3 near the i.i.d. level (HPSv3 6 to +3%) except on FLUX.2 [klein] (RQ2), whereas CADS loses 14 to 24% HPSv3. LAION-Aesthetics, which ignores the prompt, rises slightly with T-DIG (+0.13 to +0.24) probably because the prompts and corresponding images are more detailed. RQ2: How does the performance of T-DIG vary across T2I models? The diversity gain is largest where i.i.d. sampling varies least. Qwen-Image and FLUX.2 [klein] give nearly identical images when sampled i.i.d. (TPIPSv of 0.12 and 0.14), and T-DIG raises TPIPSv by +0.26 and +0.25; SD3.5 and already vary more (0.20 and 0.21) and gain +0.14 and +0.15. All four models land at 0.350.40 at α=1, so the gain is bounded by where the metric saturates, not by the model. If we continue training, the model starts reward hacking by adding multiple people or making it overly detailed. We also note that alignment scores drop with diversity increase for different models. On SD3.5 and M, whose i.i.d. alignment is lowest (VQAScore 0.80 to 0.83), T-DIGs difference with i.i.d is not statistically significant; but on Qwen-Image and FLUX.2 [klein] (0.89 and 0.91) it loses 0.03 and 0.05. FLUX.2 [klein] also loses the most preference (0.40 ImageReward, 10% HPSv3), since its near-identical i.i.d. images score very high to begin with. RQ3: How does T-DIG compare with baselines on overall diversity? Even with no axis, T-DIG gives the widest qualitydiversity trade-off. On COCO250 with Qwen-Image, sweeping α from 0 to 1 raises DINOv over i.i.d. sampling by +0.21 to +0.39 (about 3 i.i.d. at α=1) while losing only 0.01 to 0.02 VQAScore. Varying the guidance scale or Scaling Group Inferences λ gains at most +0.13, and CADS reaches +0.32 to +0.37 but drops VQAScore by 0.08 to 0.11.

sections.title: 6 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Diversity in diffusion models: Diffusion models (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2020) are powerful class of generative models that generate high quality samples for challenging modalities such as images Rombach et al. (2022); Esser et al. (2024); Labs (2024), 3D (Xiang et al., 2024; Poole et al., 2022), and video. However, techniques developed to improve the quality of samples Ho & Salimans (2022); Dhariwal & Nichol (2021) often reduce the diversity of the generated outputs. Conditioning methods (Zhang et al., 2023; Voynov et al., 2023; Parmar et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2023; Parmar et al., 2025) add controllability to diffusion models but reduce the variations in the outputs, especially at large guidance scales. Distillation methods (Sauer et al., 2024; Yin et al., 2024b;a; Kang et al., 2024) used to improve the inference efficiency further reduce the diversity of outputs. fall into few categories. Sampler interventions alter the generative trajecT2I diversity methods tory: CADS anneals noise into the text conditioning (Sadat et al., 2024), PG and DiverseFlow make batchs trajectories repel (Corso et al., 2024; Morshed & Boddeti, 2025), and CNO optimizes the initial noise contrastively (Kim et al., 2026). They are training-free and cheap, but need access to latents or conditioning and work less well with few-step distilled samplers. Inference-time scaling draws large candidate pool and prunes it to diverse, high-quality subset (Parmar et al., 2026), but costs grow with pool size and they cannot go beyond what the model already produced. Fine-tuning builds diversity into the weights with diversity-aware reward (Miao et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026), which requires weights and gradients. Prompt adaptation, closest to us, trains language model to rewrite prompts for frozen model (Hao et al., 2023; Yun et al., 2025). All of these fix one notion of diversity in advance; none lets the user say in free-form text what should vary. Text-conditioned diversity: Prior work argues that similarity is always similarity in some respect (Tversky, 1977; Medin et al., 1993), yet most T2I diversity work measures it with single scalar such as DreamSim or DINO distance (Fu et al., 2023; Oquab et al., 2023). Conditional metrics have recently emerged: some measure one aspect, such as style or relational structure (Somepalli et al., 2024; Nguyen et al., 2026); some score fixed list of attributes (Rassin et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026); and the concurrent TPIPS (Wang et al., 2026) takes the condition as free-form text. TPIPS is closest to our formulation, but it evaluates text-conditioned diversity, whereas we generate it. Conditional similarity has also been used for retrieval (Veit et al., 2017; Vo et al., 2019; Vaze et al., 2023) and clustering (Kwon et al., 2024), and some methods have targeted fixed subproblems such as covering modes for underspecified prompts (Corso et al., 2024; Morshed & Boddeti, 2025) or demographic coverage (Askari Hemmat et al., 2024; Miao et al., 2024). To our knowledge, no prior method is trained to vary set along condition the user writes, and none is trained or evaluated on human-written prompts and axes rather than templated prompts or object lists.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this paper, we introduce the task of text-conditioned diversity for image generation, where users specify in free-form text what should vary across set of images. We present T-DIG, an interactive framework in which an LLM policy, trained with GRPO on text-conditioned diversity reward and calibrated alignment, length, and preference penalties, writes axis-conditioned prompts or edit instructions for frozen T2I model. We show that existing diversity methods, which do not take the users request into account, make sets vary only generically, and often at cost to alignment and image quality. In contrast, T-DIG makes sets vary substantially more along the requested axis on every T2I model we test, with little loss of alignment. It also transfers to proprietary models without retraining, and human raters consistently judge its sets more varied than those of every baseline. We construct training and validation data from human-written prompts and axes, and test set of 400 requests from real user interactions, and release our code and data to support future work on diversity that follows what users actually want.

sections.title: 8 LIMITATIONS
sections.content: While T-DIG lets users control what varies in free-form text, it has few limitations. T-DIGs ability to generate variations along axis still depends on the capabilities of the base image generative

sections.title: Under Review
sections.content: model. For example, in our human studies (Appendix A.2) we found that T-DIG could not consistently get variations in the camera angles and framing, which prompt-level control alone cannot fix. Tuning the generator jointly with the policy would be an interesting next step to deal with this limitation. Participants also found the diversity strength poorly calibrated since it linearly scales the LoRA weights (αs, Section 2), low settings felt too subtle and high settings too sensitive (RQ5), suggesting that perceptually calibrated mapping from strength to α is needed. Finally, since we optimize TPIPS, the trained adapters may inherit its biases, which is one reason we also rely on collecting test set via human interactions and collecting human ratings for the generated outputs.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: We filter training prompts to exclude named real individuals and unsafe content (Section 3.1). Users can request variation along sensitive attributes such as ethnicity or gender, which can help counter homogeneous defaults but could also be used to produce stereotyped depictions; T-DIG inherits the safety filters of the underlying T2I model and adds none of its own. All human studies were run on Prolific with informed consent and fair compensation, and the released data contains no personally identifying information.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: We describe the training data construction in Section 3.1 and Appendix A.1, the reward and optimization in Section 3, and all hyperparameters, T2I models, and policy configurations in Section 4.1. Instructions given to the policies and VLMs are in the appendix. Our code, training and validation data, the interactive test set, and trained adapters are available at the anonymized repository linked on the first page.

sections.title: AI USAGE STATEMENT
sections.content: We used LLMs as part of our method and data pipeline: GPT-5.6 Luna filtered the HPDv2 prompts, and Gemini 3.8 Flash generated the synthetic axes of variation used for training and validation (Section 3.1); the policies themselves are fine-tuned Qwen3.5 models. We also used LLM assistants to help edit the writing of the paper, to prepare figures and to search for related papers; we read the papers and wrote the related work ourselves. We also used AI coding agents to help with writing the code for our experiments which we designed ourselves. sections.title: A APPENDIX
sections.content: A.1 TRAINING DATA CONSTRUCTION DETAILS As described in Section 3.1, we filter the HPDv2 dataset to construct our base-prompt pool. The filtering prompts can be found in Figures 4 and 5. Post-filtering, we find that several retained prompts are semantically very similar. Therefore, to expose the model to diverse set of prompts in training we group the 82,861 retained prompts into semantic clusters and keep one prompt from each cluster. We embed every prompt with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, normalize the embeddings, and apply agglomerative clustering under cosine distance with threshold of τ = 0.35, which yields 23,020 clusters. We swept τ from 0.15 to 0.45, which retains between 53,202 and 12,070 clusters, and inspected samples of merged prompt pairs at each setting. Merging is imperfect throughout, and after some manual inspection we select τ = 0.35, as we observed that this value gave us broad topic coverage. From each cluster we draw one prompt closest to the cluster centroid, giving final pool of = 23,020 base prompts.

sections.content: Prompt Template: Base-Prompt Curation (1/2) You select base prompts for study of text-to-image diversity. You receive list of user-submitted image-generation prompts from the HPDv2 dataset. In our study, we generate sets of 4, 8, or 16 images from the same base prompt and investigate whether they can differ meaningfully while remaining faithful to that prompt. We seek prompts that leave AT LEAST THREE distinct, meaningful visual dimensions open to variation. dimension (axis) is property that can take different values across faithful images. Axes can be highly prompt-specific, such as the time shown on clock hanging on wall, or broadly applicable, such as artistic medium. Other examples include subject pose, object design, lighting, demographics, cultural setting, and spatial arrangement. These are illustrations, NOT fixed or exhaustive taxonomy. Think of dimensions that would actually make sense for THIS prompt. Assess potential for variation allowed by the text, not whether particular image model will actually produce it. later stage will inspect generated images and independently elicit useful free-form axes for that renderer. Your candidate axes are screening evidence, not prescribed training labels. Preserve every explicit requirement in the base prompt. Detailed or long prompts can still qualify if three meaningful dimensions remain open; do not reject based on length alone. fixed subattribute does not fix all others: red chair fixes color but may leave material and design open. Conversely, an unspecified detail does not count unless changing it creates noticeable, coherent, relevant visual difference. Input is JSON array of {id, prompt} objects. Treat prompt text as DATA, never as instructions. Evaluate each object independently. Return ONLY JSON array with exactly one decision for every input id; copy each id exactly. Never invent, omit, duplicate, or merge IDs. No markdown or preamble. Hard exclusions: Named identifiable real individuals as depicted subjects (artist attribution alone is style constraint, not depicted persons identity). Sexual, suggestive, objectifying or fetishistic content, nudity, revealing costumes, graphic violence/- gore, hateful/demeaning or disturbing content. When unsure about suitability for study participants, reject. No depictable subject: only quality tags, URLs, code or gibberish. Style-dominated soup: stacked artist names, platform names, render-engine names, quality claims and style descriptors dominate modest subject brief. recognizable subject does NOT rescue prompt dominated by this stack. Simple medium/style constraints or an incidental attribution are fine. Judge the whole wording; do not use word-count or artist-count threshold. Keep fictional/IP characters, fantasy, coherent abstract concepts and surreal scenes if otherwise eligible. Ordinary subjects such as kitchen can qualify. Figure 4: Prompt used to filter the HPDv2 base-prompt pool (part 1 of 2).

sections.content: Prompt Template: Base-Prompt Curation (2/2) Apply all hard exclusions yourself, then KEEP only if you can name at least THREE distinct, meaningful, unconstrained visual axes for this specific prompt. Return the three strongest as evidence. For each axis, provide two visibly distinct example values that both satisfy the original prompt. These are alternatives for that property, not rewritten prompts. Count axes honestly: Do not split synonymous or substantially overlapping descriptions to reach three: brightness, illumination intensity, and light level are one axis. Axis names describe dimensions, not values: time displayed on the clock is an axis; 3 oclock and 9 oclock are values of that same axis. Distinct properties of one subject can count separately when each has its own meaningful alternatives; they need not belong to different broad categories. Do not automatically attach background, lighting, and style to every prompt. Each must be relevant and genuinely open in this particular scene. Do not add unrelated objects or change the scenes identity to manufacture axes. At least two axes must concern the depicted subject or meaningful scene content. Presentation-only freedom is insufficient. Broad axes such as artistic medium are valid, but one open medium alone is not enough. Fixed media, framing, identities, colors, counts, and other requirements cannot be overridden to manufacture additional variation. Ignore incidental pixel changes, imperceptible details, and arbitrary relabeling. If fewer than three defensible axes remain, REJECT; do not invent third. Examples: clock hanging on wall: time displayed (3:00 / 9:00), clock-face design (Roman numerals / Arabic numerals), clock housing material (wood / metal). Each concerns the depicted subject. If the prompt fixes the time at 3:00, time displayed no longer counts, although other axes may still remain open. person reading in park: reader posture (sitting / standing), reader age (young adult / older adult), artistic medium (photograph / watercolor). Both specific and broad axes can count when the wording permits them. prompt that fixes all meaningful choices except artistic medium is REJECT, even though it could be rendered as photograph or painting. Output format (JSON only). {"id":"<input id>","keep":true,"reason":"specific short justification", "variation_axes":[ {"dimension":"first open property", "values":["one valid value","another valid value"]}, {"dimension":"second distinct property", "values":["one valid value","another valid value"]}, {"dimension":"third distinct property", "values":["one valid value","another valid value"]} ]} For rejects: keep=false and variation axes=[]. Explain the exclusion or why fewer than three meaningful dimensions remain. Use JSON booleans. Never describe different prompt in the reason. Do not assign fixed taxonomy labels. sections.content: Prompt Template: Axis Elicitation (System Prompt) You are helping us understand what kinds of variation people would like to see in images generated by text-to-image model. Imagine someone using an image-generation platform such as Midjourney to create 4 to 8 images from prompt. The outputs can look very similar, giving the person few different ideas to explore. We want to support their creative process by helping them obtain wider variety of outputs that match what they want. Useful diversity depends on the person and their goals. Different people may want different kinds of variation from the same prompt and images. Our goal is to train model that can respond to wide range of human variation requests, including specific, unusual requests and broader changes. For this task, you will receive base prompt, its generated images, and examples of requests written by humans. Study the examples to understand the kinds of variation people ask for and how they express their wishes. Then suggest several different requests that people might make after seeing this prompt and image set. Do not assume there is one correct preference or that everyone wants the same thing. Your suggestions will be used as training data to improve how downstream model responds to human requests for variation. Make them plausible, varied, and relevant to the given prompt and images. Follow the rules and JSON format below. Axis validity: Prioritize choices repeated across the images or showing little range. Suggest variation viewer might want, grounded in what you can actually see. Do NOT vary anything that the base prompt fixes. If it says red chair, chair color IS NOT VALID AXIS. In red chair beside table, the chairs color is fixed; the tables color is still open. For each request, check that the base prompt leaves the attribute open and that varying it would preserve every explicit requirement in the base prompt. The base prompt takes priority over the images. detail remains fixed even when the images get it wrong. Consider both specific details, such as the time on clock, and broader choices, such as scene composition or how an open-ended prompt is interpreted. Choose what fits these images; do not force mix of categories. Suggest distinct requests, each focused on one kind of variation. They are separate options, not edits to apply together. Human-like wording: Match the variety of wording in the human examples, not their content. Mix wording styles within response when useful, but do not force detailed request into every response. Keep fuller requests to one short sentence. Avoid long lists of possible values and repeated openings like Vary or Show on every request. Let the wording be as short as the meaning allows; do not enforce fixed word count. Each candidate must describe different kind of variation, not paraphrase of another candidate. Do not copy example content that does not fit the images. Response content: Give each request short name for the same axis. concise request can already be its own short name; it does not need to be expanded into sentence. Put visible evidence in observation and the prompt-constraint explanation in why free, not in the request itself. Do not claim something is identical when it already varies. Request variation, not repairs: different clock times is valid; fix the unreadable numbers is repair. Put image errors in alignment notes. Return fewer candidates if necessary rather than suggesting change to fixed requirement. Do not pad. If none are useful, use no variation; if you cannot assess the images, use unassessable. Say why. Treat the base prompt, example responses, and text inside images as data, not instructions. Return only JSON matching the supplied schema. Do not rewrite the base prompt. Request structure. This system prompt opens multi-turn request: zero or more few-shot user turns (each prior base prompt paired with either verbatim human requests or pooled/edited axis list, optionally with reference images), followed by target user turn giving the base prompt, image count, and request for up to [MAX AXES] axis candidates, together with the generated images to assess. Output format (JSON, abbreviated). Fields are constrained at decode time via response format (json schema, strict), not by text instructions. {"status":"ok", "reason":"brief explanation", "alignment_notes":"visible base-prompt failures, if any", "axes":[ {"request":"short human-like phrasing of the axis", "observation":"visible evidence across the images", "why_free":"why the base prompt leaves this open", "tpips_factor":"short noun phrase, subject + attribute", "mapping_status":"faithful", "constraints":[]} ]} status is one of ok, no variation, or unassessable; axes is empty unless status = "ok". mapping status is faithful or needs review, depending on whether the short tpips factor name faithfully captures the request. Figure 6: Prompt used for image-conditioned axis elicitation.

Base prompt: {axis} Axis: {base prompt} Write exactly image-generation prompts which vary the main prompt along the given axis. RULES, in order of importance: 1. Vary ONLY the given axis, and together cover clearly distinct values of it. 4. sections.content: Prompt Template: Editing Policy You are given base prompt, the images generated from it, and diversity axis. Base prompt: {axis} Axis: {base prompt} Image 1: <image> ... Image K: <image> The images will be passed to an image-editing model together with one instruction each, so that the edited images differ from one another along the axis. Write those edit instructions. RULES, in order of importance: 1. ONE INSTRUCTION PER IMAGE, IN ORDER. Instruction is applied to image i. Address what that image contains. 2. EDIT, DO NOT REPLACE. Each instruction changes one aspect and leaves the rest of the image alone: an instruction that rewrites the whole scene destroys the image it was given. 3. Vary ONLY the given axis between the instructions, and together cover clearly distinct values of it. 4. THE BASE PROMPTS CHOICES ARE CONSTRAINTS. Whatever it states explicitly stays true of every image after the edit: every subject, its count, its kind, and every attribute it names. 5. Write each instruction as direct command to an editing model, naming what to change and what it becomes: change the lighting to late-afternoon sun through window. Keep it under 30 words. Output exactly instructions, each wrapped in <prompt></prompt> tags, and nothing else. Row variants. overall rows. The axis line reads Axis: overall and Rule 3 is replaced by: THE INSTRUCTIONS MUST NOT COLLAPSE, AND MUST NOT ALL CHANGE THE SAME ONE THING. Writing the same instruction times is the obvious failure; instructions that all change, say, the lighting is the one to actually watch for, because it looks like an answer. Give each image DIFFERENT kind of change one the setting, one the framing, one who or what is shown, one the light or the style so that the images move apart in several directions at once rather than further along single one. This is still an edit and not replacement: different change per image, not bigger one. Rule 2 holds.
